title: Hourly sea level at five tide gauges (Brest, Marseille, Pensacola, Manila, Fremantle), UHSLC research-quality data, year 2018

radius_enters_via.how: not the radius: the harmonic fit takes the frequency of each tidal line from the mean motions of the Moon and the Sun (Meeus); the periods read off the spectrum and the spring-neap cycle use the clock alone

verdict_rule: A tide gauge whose record has one high water per lunar day and no semidiurnal line at 12 h 25 min anywhere, or a fortnightly spring-neap cycle that does not follow the phases of the Moon, would favour a local Moon pulling water under itself over a plane.
license_note: University of Hawaii Sea Level Center data are freely available for research and education, with citation of Caldwell, Merrifield & Thompson (2015) and the UHSLC.

sources.cite: P. C. Caldwell, M. A. Merrifield, P. R. Thompson, Sea level measured by tide gauges from global oceans — the Joint Archive for Sea Level holdings (NCEI Accession 0019568), Version 5.5, NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (2015), doi:10.7289/V5V40S7W

units.year, month, day, hour: UTC (GMT), as in the UHSLC CSV
units.level: mm above the station's zero, -32767 = missing

notes: Each file is the station's whole research-quality hourly record (Brest since 1846); the build reads 2018 only, the last year every station has. Stations chosen for their kinds of tide: Brest semidiurnal and large, Marseille almost none (Mediterranean), Pensacola diurnal (Gulf of Mexico), Manila mixed, Fremantle diurnal and small (southern hemisphere).
